NOTES AND QUESTIONS
1. Before the adoption of Federal Rule 19, the principle of mandatory joinder was a judicially created doctrine. SHIELDS v. BARROW, 58 U.S.
(17 How.) 130, 15 L.Ed. 158 (1854), established that parties could be classified as necessary or indispensable depending on the nature of their
substantive rights (“joint” or “severable”). The consequences of this classification were extremely important. If an absent party who was not subject to
the jurisdiction of the court or whose joinder would destroy the pre-existing diversity of citizenship was labeled indispensable, the entire action had to
be dismissed. On the other hand, if the absentee merely was necessary, the court might exercise its discretion in determining whether or not to continue
without that person. Because a plaintiff might have been deprived of any remedy if a party was found to be indispensable, courts often strained to avoid
that conclusion. As might be suspected, this method had a debilitating effect on the standard for classification. See Comment, The Litigant and the
Absentee in Federal Multiparty Practice, 116 U.Pa.L.Rev. 531 (1968).
